rv.q: There is loss everywhere - jazz dies, his mom dies, neighborhoods change, his beloved Yankees decline and memories fade. But Crystal, under Des McAnuff's tight direction, never gets maudlin. He always knows when to dispel the darkness with a laugh...
Billy Crystal's one-man ode to his Long Island boyhood is Broadway comfort food, an irresistible combination of shtick and schmaltz. In other words, pure pleasure.
More than the ample laughs, Crystal's achievement here is in forging a tender connection to everyone who has experienced or even contemplated the loss of a parent.
We’re putty in his expert hands — and that’s the memory we’ll take with us.
Aiming for both your heartstrings and your funny bone, Crystal hits both.
The core pleasures of this warmly affectionate portrait of a New York childhood involve nostalgia and sentiment, the sex and violence of today’s Broadway.
But Crystal pushes the sentimentality so hard that it sometimes seems to break through the other side of the schmaltz-time continuum.

Seeing as few of these shows, if any, have surpassed Crystal's heartwarming and hilarious tour de force, it's a pleasure to have it return for a run before the "Les Miz" revival takes over the Imperial Theatre.
Mostly, this is a near-perfect romp through prime ethnic and distinctly New York material: religion, food, family and sports.
700 Sundays is a memory piece that pretty much remains the warmhearted, moving and extremely funny night out that it was back in 2004.

In a laugh-out-loud - if quite long - revival of his 2004 one-man, autobiographical show 700 Sundays, you can practically hear his heart soaring as he recounts wacky and sentimental stories about his childhood.
Crystal does here — and it’s more than enough.
To his great credit, he doesn't coast on his credentials. In '700 Sundays,' he delivers the full measure of his talent.
Fortunately, any hints of self-conscious, kumbaya-ish social commentary are folded seamlessly into the comedy, which is gently irreverent, endearingly good-natured and, yes, funny.

cn.t: Crystal's heartwarming and hilarious one-man show earns enthusiastic praise for its universal appeal and masterful storytelling, as the veteran entertainer delivers laugh-out-loud comedy and genuine poignancy in his moving tribute to his father.

vs.sum: The Imperial Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and solid sound quality, though some seats may miss minor stage action. While the ambiance is enhanced by its historic architectural design, comfort is average with decent legroom. Facilities are lacking, with long restroom lines being a common issue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair locations in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
